claim: Hippocampal ripples are highly synchronous neural events critical for memory consolidation and retrieval.
source: Hippocampal ripples are highly synchronous neural events critical for memory consolidation and retrieval.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of hippocampal research.

claim: A minority of strong ripples has been shown to be of particular importance in situations of increased memory demands.
source: A minority of strong ripples has been shown to be of particular importance in situations of increased memory demands.
evidence: This statement references established findings in the literature about strong ripples and memory demands.

claim: Strong ripples (top 10% in ripple strength) propagate differentially depending on their generation point along the hippocampal longitudinal axis.
source: Surprisingly, strong ripples (top 10% in ripple strength) propagate differentially depending on their generation point along the hippocampal longitudinal axis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The septal hippocampal pole is able to generate longer ripples that engage more neurons and elicit spiking activity for an extended time even at considerable distances.
source: The septal hippocampal pole is able to generate longer ripples that engage more neurons and elicit spiking activity for an extended time even at considerable distances.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A substantial portion of the variance in strong ripple duration (R² = 0.463) is explained by the ripple generation location on the longitudinal axis.
source: Accordingly, a substantial portion of the variance in strong ripple duration (R² = 0.463) is explained by the ripple generation location on the longitudinal axis, in agreement with a possible distinctive role of the hippocampal septal pole in conditions of high-memory demand.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The location of the ripple generation has a significant impact on the spiking rate modulation of different hippocampal subfields, even before the onset of the ripple.
source: Moreover, we observed that the location of the ripple generation has a significant impact on the spiking rate modulation of different hippocampal subfields, even before the onset of the ripple.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hippocampal ripples are brief oscillatory events detected in the local field potential (LFP) of the hippocampal formation.
source: Hippocampal ripples are brief oscillatory events detected in the local field potential (LFP) of the hippocampal formation, these events correspond to the synchronized depolarization of a substantial number of neurons in various hippocampal subregions (Hulse et al., 2016; Ylinen et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Higher ripple incidence during memory encoding is associated with superior recall performance.
source: An higher ripple incidence during memory encoding is associated with superior recall performance (Norman et al., 2019), furthermore, ripple incidence is increased during successful memory retrieval (Carr et al., 2011; Vaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ripple incidence is increased during successful memory retrieval.
source: An higher ripple incidence during memory encoding is associated with superior recall performance (Norman et al., 2019), furthermore, ripple incidence is increased during successful memory retrieval (Carr et al., 2011; Vaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ripples are involved in memory consolidation both in awake and sleep conditions.
source: Ripples are also involved in memory consolidation both in awake and sleep conditions (Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012; Roux et al., 2017; Sirota et al., 2003), disrupting awake ripples during learning causes a persisting performance degradation, the same effect can be achieved by silencing ripples during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Disrupting awake ripples during learning causes a persisting performance degradation.
source: Ripples are also involved in memory consolidation both in awake and sleep conditions (Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012; Roux et al., 2017; Sirota et al., 2003), disrupting awake ripples during learning causes a persisting performance degradation, the same effect can be achieved by silencing ripples during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Silencing ripples during post-learning sleep causes performance degradation.
source: Ripples are also involved in memory consolidation both in awake and sleep conditions (Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012; Roux et al., 2017; Sirota et al., 2003), disrupting awake ripples during learning causes a persisting performance degradation, the same effect can be achieved by silencing ripples during post-learning sleep.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ripples are considered to play a crucial role in memory processes and reorganization of memory engrams.
source: Accordingly, ripples are considered to play a crucial role in memory processes and reorganization of memory engrams (Buzsáki, 2015; Davidson et al., 2009; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Girardeau et al., 2009; Girardeau and Zugaro, 2011; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015; Takahashi, 2015; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Ripple duration exhibits a skewed distribution with only a minority of long-duration ripples (>100 ms).
source: Ripples duration exhibits a skewed distribution with only a minority of long-duration ripples (>100 ms).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about ripple characteristics based on established knowledge.

claim: The fraction of long-duration ripples, ripple amplitude, and within-ripple firing rate of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons are increased in both novel contexts and memory-demanding tasks.
source: The fraction of long-duration ripples, ripple amplitude, and within-ripple firing rate of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons are increased in both novel contexts and memory-demanding tasks (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reducing ripple duration artificially causes a degraded working memory performance.
source: Reducing ripple duration artificially causes a degraded working memory performance (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Jadhav et al., 2012) and, on the contrary, prolongation induced by optogenetic activation has a beneficial effect (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prolongation of ripple duration induced by optogenetic activation has a beneficial effect on memory performance.
source: Reducing ripple duration artificially causes a degraded working memory performance (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Jadhav et al., 2012) and, on the contrary, prolongation induced by optogenetic activation has a beneficial effect (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The artificial recruitment of additional neurons seems to be constrained by pre-existing resting potential dynamics.
source: Importantly, the artificial recruitment of additional neurons seems to be constrained by pre-existing resting potential dynamics (Noguchi et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hippocampal–neocortical interactions are increased specifically during long-duration compared to short-duration ripples.
source: Hippocampal–neocortical interactions, suggested to be important for memory consolidation (Gais et al., 2007; Klinzing et al., 2019; Tukker et al., 2020), are increased specifically during long-duration compared to short-duration ripples (Ngo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ripple amplitude and duration are significantly correlated.
source: Ripple amplitude and duration are significantly correlated (Patel et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2021), moreover, they are both related to the amount of underlying spiking activity (Khodagholy et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ripple amplitude and duration are both related to the amount of underlying spiking activity.
source: Ripple amplitude and duration are significantly correlated (Patel et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2021), moreover, they are both related to the amount of underlying spiking activity (Khodagholy et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is possible to combine ripple strength and amplitude by considering the area of the high-pass filtered envelope (ripple strength).
source: It is possible to combine ripple strength and amplitude by considering the area of the high-pass filtered envelope (ripple strength).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing how ripple strength is calculated.

claim: Hippocampal connectivity with cortical and subcortical areas varies considerably along the longitudinal axis.
source: Hippocampal connectivity with cortical and subcortical areas varies considerably along the longitudinal axis (Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Moser and Moser, 1998) and gene expression, as well, exhibits both gradual and discrete transitions along the same axis (Strange et al., 2014; Vogel et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gene expression exhibits both gradual and discrete transitions along the hippocampal longitudinal axis.
source: Hippocampal connectivity with cortical and subcortical areas varies considerably along the longitudinal axis (Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Moser and Moser, 1998) and gene expression, as well, exhibits both gradual and discrete transitions along the same axis (Strange et al., 2014; Vogel et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hippocampus is considered to be functionally segmented along its long axis.
source: Consequently, the hippocampus is considered to be functionally segmented along its long axis.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The different connectivity contributes to explain the functional organization gradient between a predominantly spatio-visual (septal pole) and emotional (temporal pole) processing.
source: The different connectivity contributes to explain the functional organization gradient between a predominantly spatio-visual (septal pole) and emotional (temporal pole) processing.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about hippocampal functional organization.

claim: Ripples generated in the septal and temporal hippocampal pole have been shown to be temporally independent and able to engage different neuron subpopulations, even in the same downstream brain area.
source: Ripples generated in the septal and temporal hippocampal pole have already been shown to be temporally independent and able to engage different neuron subpopulations, even in the same downstream brain area (Sosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A heterogeneous ripple generation chance along the longitudinal axis most probably has an impact on the frequency with which different brain areas and neurons subgroups are activated by ripples.
source: Consequentially, a heterogeneous ripple generation chance along the longitudinal axis most probably has an impact on the frequency with which different brain areas and neurons subgroups are activated by ripples.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previous statement about ripple generation.

claim: The dataset analyzed comprises 267 Neuropixel recordings in 49 awake, head-fixed mice.
source: We analyzed ripple propagation within the hippocampal formation in a large open-access dataset comprising 267 Neuropixel recordings in 49 awake, head-fixed mice.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: Distance between recording locations explains 57.6% of the variability in ripple strength correlation.
source: Distance between recording location could explain the majority (57.6%) of this variability (Figure 1B) with the top and bottom quartiles of ripple strength correlation showing significantly different average distances (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Almost half of the ripples in long-distance pairs (49.3 ± 2.2%) were detected in both locations.
source: Almost half of the ripples in long-distance pairs (49.3 ± 2.2%) were detected in both locations (inside a 120-ms window centered on ripple start at the reference location).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Short-distance pairs showed a more reliable propagation (69.59 ± 3.51%) compared to long-distance pairs.
source: Unsurprisingly short-distance pairs showed a more reliable propagation (69.59 ± 3.51%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Strong ripples identified in the medial section showed a markedly positive lag (lag = 17.83 ± 1.02 ms) indicative of a preferred medial→lateral traveling direction.
source: Strong ripples identified in the medial section, in opposition to common ripples, showed a markedly positive lag (lag = 17.83 ± 1.02 ms) indicative of a preferred medial→lateral traveling direction (Figure 1H top).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Strong ripples identified in the lateral section did not show a markedly positive lag (lag = 3.62 ± 1.05 ms).
source: Surprisingly, the same was not true for strong ripples identified in the lateral section (lag = 3.62 ± 1.05 ms, Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Ripple strength correlates significantly better with the hippocampal population spiking rate on a ripple-to-ripple basis compared to ripple duration alone (p-value = 4.31e−11).
source: Notably ripple strength correlates significantly better with the hippocampal population spiking rate on a ripple-to-ripple basis compared to ripple duration alone (p-value = 4.31e−11, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Clear ripples were observed uniquely in the hippocampal formation (CA1, CA2, CA3, DG, SUB, and ProS).
source: Clear ripples were observed uniquely in the hippocampal formation (CA1, CA2, CA3, DG, SUB, and ProS).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The vast majority of the variance in 3D distance between recording locations was explained by the distance on the medio-lateral (M-L) axis alone (R² = 0.899).
source: The vast majority of the variance in 3D distance between recording locations was explained by the distance on the medio-lateral (M-L) axis alone (R² = 0.899).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: In common ripples, regardless of the reference location, most ripples started from the lateral section.
source: In common ripples, regardless of the reference location, most ripples started from the lateral section (Figure 3A left).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In all hippocampal sections, the majority of strong ripples are locally generated.
source: We identified two principles relative to strong ripples generation: In all hippocampal sections, the majority of strong ripples are locally generated, and a greater number of strong ripples is generated medially than laterally.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: A greater number of strong ripples is generated medially than laterally.
source: We identified two principles relative to strong ripples generation: In all hippocampal sections, the majority of strong ripples are locally generated, and a greater number of strong ripples is generated medially than laterally.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Ripples generated laterally were effectively less able to retain their strength propagating toward the medial pole.
source: We observed that ripples generated laterally were effectively less able to retain their strength propagating toward the medial pole (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No gradient in ripple strength was observed along the M-L axis (R²=0.0012).
source: This result is not simply explained by differences in ripple strength along the M-L axis, as no such gradient was observed (R²=0.0012, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ripple amplitude showed a weak trend with higher amplitude ripples in the lateral section (r = 0.27, p-value = 1.62e−04).
source: Curiously, ripple amplitude showed a weak trend in the opposite direction (r = 0.27, p-value = 1.62e−04), with higher amplitude ripples in the lateral section (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the 50- to 120-ms window post-ripple start (late phase), medial ripples could elicit significantly higher spiking activity than lateral ripples along the entire M-L axis.
source: Surprisingly, in the 50- to 120-ms window post-ripple start (late phase), medial ripples could elicit significantly higher spiking activity than lateral ripples along the entire M-L axis (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The medial hippocampal section is able to generate longer ripples.
source: In accordance with this result, we found that the medial hippocampal section is able to generate longer ripples (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: An important portion of the variance in ripple duration is explained by location on the M-L axis both in common (R² = 0.133) and especially in strong ripples (R² = 0.463).
source: An important portion of the variance in ripple duration is indeed explained by location on the M-L axis both in common (R² = 0.133) and especially in strong ripples (R² = 0.463).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Fraction of active neurons and spiking rate were both significantly higher in medial ripples.
source: Fraction of active neurons and spiking rate were both significantly higher in medial ripples (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the late phase, the difference in fraction of active neurons per ripples between medial and lateral ripples was striking (Cohen's d = 1.7).
source: Focusing only on the late phase the difference in fraction of active neurons per ripples between medial and lateral ripples was even more striking (Cohen's d = 1.7, Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: In the early phase, lateral ripples could engage more neurons, although the effect size was much smaller (Cohen's d=0.39).
source: Inversely, in the early phase, lateral ripples could engage more neurons, although, the effect size was much smaller (Cohen's d=0.39).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Medial ripples caused a significant and considerable increase in spiking rate in the late phase (Cohen's d = 1.75).
source: The same result was found in relation to the spiking rate, medial ripples caused a significant and considerable increase in spiking rate in the late phase (Cohen's d = 1.75, Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Differences in firing rate, waveform duration, and waveform shape (recovery slope and peak-trough ratio) were found in putative excitatory neurons across hippocampal sections.
source: We did not find differences in the number of firing neurons across the CA1 subfield (medial = 74.16, lateral = 69.66, p-value = 9.48e−01, Mann–Whitney U test), we did, however, found differences in firing rate, waveform duration, and waveform shape (recovery slope and peak-trough ratio, Figure 4—figure supplement 4) in putative excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Firing rate and waveform duration in putative excitatory neurons exhibited, respectively, a left- and right-shifted distribution in the lateral section, reflecting lower firing rate and slower action potentials.
source: Firing rate and waveform duration in putative excitatory neurons exhibited, respectively, a left- and right-shifted distribution in the lateral section, reflecting lower firing rate and slower action potentials.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Putative inhibitory interneurons in the lateral section showed a higher firing rate.
source: Putative inhibitory interneurons in the lateral section showed a higher firing rate.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Clusters located in the thalamus (TH) and midbrain (MB) were hardly modulated (MB: 0.85 ± 0.71%, TH: 0.0 ± 0.0%).
source: We found that clusters located in the thalamus (TH) and midbrain (MB) were hardly modulated (MB: 0.85 ± 0.71%, TH: 0.0 ± 0.0%), with baseline spiking rate explaining nearly all the variance in spiking rate during ripples (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Only a small fraction of cortical clusters were modulated (Isocortex: 5.26 ± 0.97%).
source: Only a small fraction of cortical clusters were modulated (Isocortex: 5.26 ± 0.97%), in contrast, the majority of hippocampal (HPF) clusters showed ripple modulation (HPF: 88.57 ± 1.03%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The majority of hippocampal (HPF) clusters showed ripple modulation (HPF: 88.57 ± 1.03%).
source: Only a small fraction of cortical clusters were modulated (Isocortex: 5.26 ± 0.97%), in contrast, the majority of hippocampal (HPF) clusters showed ripple modulation (HPF: 88.57 ± 1.03%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: In the 50- to 120-ms window, medial ripples showed a notably stronger modulatory effect.
source: A stronger effect was observed when isolating early and late phase. For example, in the 50- to 120-ms window medial ripples showed a notably stronger modulatory effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Significant differences were observed in cortical clusters and in TH, with medial ripples inducing stronger modulation.
source: Significant differences were also observed in cortical clusters and in TH, with medial ripples inducing stronger modulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In the early phase, lateral ripples showed significantly stronger engagement of the dentate gyrus (DG), CA1 and CA3 areas and weaker engagement of the subiculum (SUB).
source: In the early phase, we found a significantly stronger engagement of the dentate gyrus (DG), CA1 and CA3 areas and weaker engagement of the subiculum (SUB) by lateral ripples.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: In the late phase, CA1, CA3, DG, prosubiculum (ProS), and SUB all displayed stronger modulation in response to medial ripples.
source: The late phase analysis revealed further differences, as CA1, CA3, DG, prosubiculum (ProS), and SUB all displayed stronger modulation in response to medial ripples (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Prior to the onset of ripples (20-ms window), medial ripples induced stronger modulation in ProS and SUB, weaker modulation in DG and substantially weaker modulation in CA3 when compared to lateral ripples.
source: Additionally, we found that prior to the onset of ripples (20-ms window), medial ripple-induced stronger modulation in ProS and SUB, weaker modulation in DG and substantially weaker modulation in CA3 when compared to lateral ripples (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The majority of clusters did not display a strong preference for medial or lateral ripples (84.29%).
source: Our analysis revealed that the majority of clusters did not display a strong preference (84.29%), whereas 10.4% of clusters responded preferentially to lateral ripples and 5.31% to medial ripples (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: 10.4% of clusters responded preferentially to lateral ripples and 5.31% to medial ripples.
source: Our analysis revealed that the majority of clusters did not display a strong preference (84.29%), whereas 10.4% of clusters responded preferentially to lateral ripples and 5.31% to medial ripples (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: DG exhibited the highest proportion (28.15%) of neurons responsive to lateral ripples.
source: Specifically, DG exhibited the highest proportion (28.15%) of neurons responsive to lateral ripples.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: SUB displayed the highest proportion (11.68%) of neurons responsive to medial ripples.
source: In contrast, SUB displayed the highest proportion (11.68%) of neurons responsive to medial ripples (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Strong ripples propagate differentially along the hippocampal longitudinal axis for the first time.
source: Our results show for the first time that strong ripples propagate differentially along the hippocampal longitudinal axis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the data analysis.

claim: It was previously observed that ripples located at the septal and temporal pole are generated independently from each other.
source: It was previously observed that ripples located at the septal and temporal pole are generated independently from each other, in addition, despite the presence of connections within the hippocampal longitudinal axis (van Strien et al., 2009; Witter, 2007), in the vast majority of cases ripples do not propagate to the opposite pole (Sosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the vast majority of cases ripples do not propagate to the opposite pole.
source: It was previously observed that ripples located at the septal and temporal pole are generated independently from each other, in addition, despite the presence of connections within the hippocampal longitudinal axis (van Strien et al., 2009; Witter, 2007), in the vast majority of cases ripples do not propagate to the opposite pole (Sosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Only half of the ripples generated in the septal pole were detected additionally in the intermediate hippocampus (lateral section).
source: The effect of distance was also apparent on the ripple chance of propagation, only half of the ripples generated in the septal pole were detected additionally in the intermediate hippocampus (lateral section in our analysis).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: This chance is much higher compared to the ~3.7% reported regarding propagation between opposite poles.
source: This chance is much higher compared to the ~3.7% reported regarding propagation between opposite poles (Sosa et al., 2020), it would be interesting to understand whether the temporal pole is also able to entrain the intermediate hippocampus in similar fashion or it is a peculiarity of the septal pole.
evidence: This statement compares the current findings with previous research cited.

claim: Ripples can arise at any location along the hippocampal longitudinal axis.
source: Ripples can arise at any location along the hippocampal longitudinal axis (Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Ripples are not homogeneously generated across space.
source: Our analysis shows that ripples are, however, not homogeneously generated across space.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Common ripples followed a gradient with higher generation probability in the intermediate section and lowest in the septal pole.
source: Common ripples followed a gradient with higher generation probability in the intermediate section and lowest in the septal pole.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Only rarely a strong ripple generated in the intermediate hippocampus is able to propagate toward the septal pole retaining its strong status (top 10%).
source: Furthermore, only rarely a strong ripple generated in the intermediate hippocampus is able to propagate toward the septal pole retaining its strong status (top 10%).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Strong ripples generated in the septal pole have a significantly higher chance of propagate longitudinally and still be in the top 10% in terms of ripple strength.
source: Conversely strong ripples generated in the septal pole have a significantly higher chance of propagate longitudinally and still be in the top 10% in terms of ripple strength.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: No difference in ripple strength was observed along the longitudinal axis.
source: Notably, this is not consequence of a simple longitudinal gradient in ripple strength, indeed, we did not observe any difference in ripple strength along the longitudinal axis.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The temporal hippocampus has been shown to produce shorter ripples both in awake and sleep conditions.
source: Consistent with a duration gradient along the longitudinal axis, the temporal hippocampus has been shown to produce shorter ripples both in awake and sleep conditions (Sosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Slower action potentials and longer refractory periods may hinder the ability to sustain protracted high frequency spiking.
source: We can hypothesize that slower action potentials and, consequentially, longer refractory periods hinder the ability to sustain protracted high frequency spiking.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the observed electrophysiological differences.

claim: The neuromodulatory inputs gradient might influence neurons responses.
source: We can also speculate that the neuromodulatory inputs gradient, monoamine fibers have been shown to be stronger in the ventral part (Strange et al., 2014), might influence neurons responses.
evidence: This is speculation based on known neuromodulatory gradients.

claim: Serotonin, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine have all been shown to suppress ripples.
source: Serotonin (ul Haq et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015), noradrenaline (Novitskaya et al., 2016; Ul Haq et al., 2012), and acetylcholine Zhang et al., 2021 have all been shown to suppress ripples.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some ripples are coupled with a reduced activation of the locus coeruleus and the dorsal raphe nucleus in vivo.
source: In accordance with this, some ripples are coupled with a reduced activation of the locus coeruleus and the dorsal raphe nucleus in vivo (Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Ripples can be subdivided in different types according to the relationship between the hippocampal LFP and the ripple itself.
source: Ripple amplitude and duration are significantly correlated (Patel et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2021), moreover, they are both related to the amount of underlying spiking activity (Khodagholy et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2021). It is possible to combine ripple strength and amplitude by considering the area of the high-pass filtered envelope (ripple strength).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different ripple subtypes are associated with two different brain-wide networks.
source: Intriguingly, these subtypes are associated with two different brain-wide networks, the first communicating preferentially with the associative neocortex and a second one biased toward subcortical structures.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about ripple subtypes.

claim: Different types of ripples have been proposed to possibly fulfill different functional roles.
source: Moreover, these different types of ripples have been proposed to possibly fulfill different functional roles.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about ripple subtypes.

claim: Ripple generated at different points of the hippocampal longitudinal axis might have functional differences.
source: Given the different input/output connectivity between septal, intermediate, and temporal hippocampus (Fanselow and Dong, 2010) we hypothesize that ripple generated at different points of the hippocampal longitudinal axis might as well have functional differences, with the longer ripples generated septally possibly able to combine the different kind of information processed in the distinct hippocampal sections and additionally relaying the integrated information back to the neocortex in accordance with the two-stage memory hypothesis (Buzsáki, 1989; Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Marr, 1971; McClelland et al., 1995; Rasch and Born, 2007).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from known connectivity patterns and memory theories.

claim: Long-duration ripples have been shown to be of particular importance in situations of high-memory demand.
source: Long-duration ripples have been shown to be of particular importance in situations of high-memory demand (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019), at the same time, previous studies highlighted the role of septal hippocampus in memory tasks and information processing (Bradfield et al., 2020; Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Hock and Bunsey, 1998; Kheirbek et al., 2013; Maras et al., 2014; McGlinchey and Aston-Jones, 2018; Moser et al., 1993; Moser et al., 1995; Qin et al., 2021; Steffenach et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies highlighted the role of septal hippocampus in memory tasks and information processing.
source: Long-duration ripples have been shown to be of particular importance in situations of high-memory demand (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019), at the same time, previous studies highlighted the role of septal hippocampus in memory tasks and information processing (Bradfield et al., 2020; Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Hock and Bunsey, 1998; Kheirbek et al., 2013; Maras et al., 2014; McGlinchey and Aston-Jones, 2018; Moser et al., 1993; Moser et al., 1995; Qin et al., 2021; Steffenach et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The results can contribute to explain the specific role of septal hippocampus in memory-demanding tasks with its ability of generating particularly long ripples.
source: Our results can contribute to explain the specific role of septal hippocampus in memory-demanding tasks with its ability of generating particularly long ripples that are able to strongly engage networks in the entire top half of the hippocampal formation for an extended time.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study's findings to the known role of the septal hippocampus.

claim: CA3 may play a more critical role in initiating lateral ripples, in accordance with the traditional view that CA3 is the primary generator of ripples.
source: These results indicate that CA3 may play a more critical role in initiating lateral ripples, in accordance with the traditional view that CA3 is the primary generator of ripples (Buzsáki, 1986; Buzsáki, 1989; Csicsvari et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Medial ripples demonstrate stronger engagement of ProS and SUB subfields before ripple start, supporting the hypothesis that output structures in the hippocampus are also capable of generating ripples.
source: On the other hand, medial ripples demonstrate stronger engagement of ProS and SUB subfields before ripple start, supporting the more recent hypothesis that output structures in the hippocampus are also capable of generating ripples (Imbrosci et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis, supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The weaker engagement of the subiculum during lateral ripples may reflect a more localized processing of information within the hippocampus.
source: It is possible that the weaker engagement of the subiculum during lateral ripples may reflect a more localized processing of information within the hippocampus, while the stronger engagement of the subiculum during medial ripples may reflect a more global transfer of information to other brain regions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in subiculum engagement.

claim: The stronger engagement of the subiculum during medial ripples may reflect a more global transfer of information to other brain regions.
source: It is possible that the weaker engagement of the subiculum during lateral ripples may reflect a more localized processing of information within the hippocampus, while the stronger engagement of the subiculum during medial ripples may reflect a more global transfer of information to other brain regions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in subiculum engagement.

claim: Six sessions were excluded because of absence of recording electrodes in CA1.
source: We excluded six sessions because of absence of recording electrodes in CA1 (session ids = 732592105, 737581020, 739448407, 742951821, 760693773, 762120172).

claim: One session was excluded because of an artifact in the LFP time series.
source: Furthermore, one session was excluded (session id = 743475441) because of an artifact in the LFP time series (time was not monotonically increasing) and two other sessions (session ids = 746083955, 756029989) because of duplicated LFP traces (see https://github.com/RobertoDF/Allen_visual_dataset_artifacts).
evidence: This is a description of the data exclusion criteria.

claim: The analysis was focused on 49 sessions.
source: Our analysis was therefore focused on 49 sessions, average animal age = 119.22 ± 1.81.
evidence: This is a description of the final dataset used in the study.

claim: Ripples were detected on CA1 LFP traces using a sixth-order Butterworth bandpass filter between 120.0 and 250.0 Hz.
source: The LFP traces sampled at 1250 Hz were filtered using a sixth-order Butterworth bandpass filter between 120.0 and 250.0. Ripples were detected on CA1 LFP traces, the best channel (higher ripple strength) was selected by looking at the SD of the envelope of the filtered trace, if multiple SD peaks were present across space (possibly caused by sharp waves in stratum radiatum and ripple activity in stratum pyramidale) we subsequently looked at the channel with higher skewness, in this way we could reliably identify the best ripple channel.
evidence: This is a description of the ripple detection methodology.

claim: Ripple threshold was set at 5 SDs.
source: Ripple threshold was set at 5 SDs.
evidence: This is a description of the ripple detection methodology.

claim: Ripple duration was limited at >0.015 and <0.25 s.
source: Ripple duration was limited at >0.015 and <0.25 s.
evidence: This is a description of the ripple detection methodology.

claim: Ripple candidates detected during running epochs were discarded.
source: Ripple candidates detected during running epochs were discarded, an animal was considered to be running if his standardized speed was higher than the 10th percentile plus 0.06.
evidence: This is a description of the ripple detection methodology.
